payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

On 2026-08-16 a stray 7.6 MB SQLite file was left at `.beads/beads.db.recovered` during a tracker repair. It was never staged by hand. The next ship advance committed it:

    git log --oneline -- .beads/beads.db.recovered
    910b0dd chore(beads): close the shipped track (basicly-e2mz.16)

    git cat-file -s $(git rev-parse HEAD:.beads/beads.db.recovered)
    7.6 MB

Observed: the engine tracker-state rollup stages the whole `.beads/` directory, so any file under it that the ignore rules miss enters a commit.

Expected: the rollup stages the known tracker paths only, and never a directory glob.

## Why the ignore rules missed it

`.beads/.gitignore` carries `*.db`, `*.db-shm`, `*.db-wal`. A name ending `.recovered` matches none of them, confirmed with `git check-ignore -v` returning NOT IGNORED. The ignore list is a denylist of suffixes, so it can only ever catch names someone predicted.

## The second-order damage

Deleting the stray broke 37 tests at once. The `work_repo` fixture copies tracked files, so a tracked-then-deleted path raises FileNotFoundError during fixture setup, and every test using that fixture errors. The blast radius of a stray file is therefore the whole suite, not one assertion.

The 7.6 MB blob remains in git history. Removing it needs a history rewrite, which is the owner decision, and is probably not worth it for one blob.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a file under the tracker directory that is neither tracker state nor ignored when the tracker state rollup runs then the rollup shall not stage it, and shall name it as unexpected rather than committing it
- Given the known tracker state paths are dirty when the rollup runs then it shall stage exactly those paths

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

payload.title: tracker adopt reconciles records but leaves an edge the ledger never saw

payload.text:
## Steps to Reproduce

Measured 2026-08-16, after filing six beads with raw br create and raw br dep add rather than through the seam.

    uv run basicly tracker adopt
    adopted 6 record(s): basicly-e2mz.28, basicly-e2mz.33, basicly-e2mz.34, basicly-e2mz.35, basicly-vkh0.30, basicly-vkh0.31

    uv run basicly tracker shadow
    31 record(s) in scope, 9 of them adopted; 866 imported, 0 declared
      disagreement: record='basicly-vkh0.27', query='ready', owned=True, reference=False
      disagreement: record='basicly-vkh0.29', query='ready', owned=True, reference=False
    clean: no · conclusive: yes

Adoption removed every record absence. The two survivors are both the same shape: the owned store reports the issue ready, the reference reports it blocked, because the blocker EDGE is in br and not in the ledger. Adopt reconciles records and not edges.

## Why no seam-routed command can repair it

    uv run basicly tracker write -- dep add basicly-vkh0.27 basicly-vkh0.26 --type blocks
    Dependency already exists: basicly-vkh0.27 → basicly-vkh0.26

The mirror writes only on an ACCEPTED br write. br rejects the duplicate, so nothing is mirrored, and the ledger stays short of the edge forever. Once br holds an edge the ledger never saw, the seam is structurally unable to reconcile it.

## Evidence that this is the operator bypass and not a mirror defect

Records filed through the seam carry the full event set; records filed with raw br create carry none of it. Measured over the ledger:

    seam-routed  e2mz.29  created 1, status 1, edge 2, comment 1
    seam-routed  e2mz.31  created 1, status 1, edge 2, comment 1
    raw br       vkh0.27  field 1
    raw br       vkh0.29  field 1
    raw br       vkh0.30  NONE

The mirror is behaving exactly as designed. The gap is that adopt, the verb whose stated job is reconciling what a hand-run br created, covers only half of what a hand-run br creates.

## Why it matters now

These two disagreements are the whole distance between the differential reading clean and not clean, and a clean conclusive run is what licenses the flip. The cutover is blocked on a reconciliation gap rather than on any remaining engineering.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a dependency edge the reference holds and the owned ledger does not when tracker adopt runs then the edge is appended to the ledger and the differential reports no disagreement for that record
- Given an edge present in both stores when adopt runs then nothing is appended, so a second run changes nothing

## Scope

- `src/basicly/tracker_cutover.py`
- `tests/test_tracker_adoption.py`

payload.title: redaction does not catch an environment dump

payload.name: description
payload.value:
## Steps to Reproduce

On 2026-08-16 a comment body was passed to the shell inside double quotes with backticks in it. zsh ran the backticked words as command substitution, and one expanded the whole shell environment into the comment: 152 environment variable assignments, 40325 characters, including a live 32-character CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN.

The write went through the seam, so it reached both stores.

Redaction was then run explicitly and changed nothing relevant:

    uv run python -c "... b.scrub_export(...), b.scrub_ledger(...)"
    scrubbed: 898 0

    grep -c CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN .beads/issues.jsonl .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl
    .beads/issues.jsonl:1
    .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl:1

Expected: a NAME=value block carrying a token-shaped value is redacted at the write, before it enters either store.

## Why the existing rules missed it

The architecture states three rule sets: high-signal secret shapes, machine path shapes, and the running user's own name. An environment dump matches none of them. The token is not in a recognised credential format, the assignment is not a path, and the variable names are not the username.

The value that leaked was 32 characters of hex with no prefix. A shape-matcher keyed on known credential prefixes cannot see it. What identifies it is the CONTEXT - an uppercase identifier ending in TOKEN, SECRET, KEY or PASSWORD, followed by an equals sign and a non-trivial value.

## What did not leak

Checked by name: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GITHUB_TOKEN and OPENAI_API_KEY were all absent. The exposure was a local session IPC token, plus machine paths and environment variable names.

## Why this was recoverable, and why that is luck

Nothing had been committed. HEAD held zero occurrences, so the repair was an edit to two uncommitted working files. Had a commit intervened, the remedy would have been a history rewrite.

A lane was running at the time and the loop commits tracker state at arbitrary points, so the window was minutes wide. Recovery depended on noticing before an unrelated process committed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a write whose body contains an uppercase identifier ending in TOKEN, SECRET, KEY or PASSWORD followed by an equals sign and a value when redaction runs then the value is replaced with a labelled placeholder before the write enters either store
- Given a write body carrying a large block of NAME=value lines when redaction runs then the block is refused or redacted rather than stored verbatim
- Given a body with no such pattern then redaction changes nothing, proven by a positive control

## Scope

- `src/basicly/redact.py`
- `tests/test_redact.py`

payload.title: neither store can remove a record once written, and one of them must be able to

payload.name: description
payload.value:
## Steps to Reproduce

A comment written on 2026-08-16 carried a leaked environment dump into both stores. Removing it was necessary and neither store offered a way.

    uv run br comments --help
    Commands: add, list, help

There is no delete. The owned ledger is append-only by design, so it has no removal either.

The repair was a hand edit of two uncommitted working files, verified afterwards:

    .beads/issues.jsonl        898 valid records, 0 occurrences
    .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl  5294 valid events, 0 occurrences

That is only defensible because nothing had been committed. Had it been, the remedy would have been a history rewrite of a tracked store, which is an owner decision and a bad one to be forced into.

## The tension, stated rather than resolved

Append-only is the ledger's integrity property and the reason a fold has authority. The architecture is explicit: repairs are corrective appends, a broken log is reported and never rewritten in place. That rule is right for a wrong FACT.

It is not sufficient for a wrong DISCLOSURE. A corrective append leaves the secret readable in the file. Redaction after the fact needs the bytes to change, which is exactly what append-only forbids.

So the two properties genuinely conflict, and the resolution is a design question rather than a bug fix. Candidates, none chosen here:

1. A redaction event that the fold honours, plus a compaction step that is the only writer permitted to rewrite history, run deliberately and leaving evidence that it ran.
2. Refuse at the write. If nothing unredactable can enter, nothing needs removing. This is basicly-vkh0.33 and it is the cheaper half, but it only covers shapes someone predicted.
3. Accept that removal requires a rewrite, and make that a first-class, audited operation rather than a hand edit under time pressure.

Option 2 alone is not enough: it fails exactly when the shape is novel, which is the case that produced this bead.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a record or event whose content must be withdrawn when the withdrawal path runs then the content is unreadable in the store afterwards and the fold reports that a withdrawal occurred, with its time and reason
- Given the withdrawal path when it runs then it is the only code permitted to rewrite the log, and a consistency check afterwards reports the log as sound

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py`
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/fsck.py`
- `tests/test_kit_tracker_events.py`

claims.claim: A leaked disclosure can be withdrawn from the tracker ledger
`events.withdraw` takes one event's free text out, keeps every value the fold reads by name, re-mints the id and appends a `withdrawn` event whose time and reason the fold reports.

body.post_ship_action: Before the tag moves, the two unsupported sentences are the owner's call to correct in `changelog.d/basicly-vkh0.34.added.md`, since a false capability claim in release notes is caught by a consumer and by no gate we run; the accurate narrower statements are that `events.withdraw` is the only rewriter in the tracker kit and that `fsck` reports a line whose record, kind or payload was edited in place without re-minting the id. After the tag moves I will file two records against basicly-vkh0: one to reconcile the exclusivity claim with `src/basicly/tracker.py:819` scrub_ledger — either by routing the scrub through the withdrawal path or by narrowing the published claim and adding a gate that enumerates in-place writers so a third one cannot appear unannounced; and one for the reproduced defect where `fsck` reports a withdrawn log clean while `scrub_ledger` raises TrackerDivergenceError on the same file, because `fsck` matches an id at any generation while `scrub_ledger` derives it densely, which wedges the engine's tracker-commit path for a record holding two identical-payload events whose earlier generation was withdrawn. Neither record blocks this release; both are opened before basicly-hnnmk9 proceeds, since it depends on this one and inherits the exclusivity premise.

unsupported.claim: and only that path may rewrite it
unsupported.why: I looked for a gate or test asserting that `events.withdraw` is the sole in-place rewriter of the ledger and found the opposite in the same tree: `src/basicly/tracker.py:819` defines `scrub_ledger`, whose own docstring at line 827 calls it 'The one place this design edits a line rather than appending one', and which rewrites `actor` and `payload` and re-dumps the line at tracker.py:892-907 over the same `.basicly/ledger/events-*.jsonl` store. It is not hypothetical: `src/basicly/merge.py:667` invokes it on what that call site calls 'the engine's only tracker-commit path', so a second path rewrites the log on every engine tracker commit. No test or gate binds the exclusivity, and because `scrub_ledger` re-mints the id it is invisible to the new `unminted-id` check as well.

unsupported.claim: `fsck` now reports any line edited in place by anything else.
unsupported.why: The word 'any' overstates the check by two margins I confirmed by running it. First, `events.event_id_for` digests only record, kind and payload — its docstring at events.py:534-536 says 'nothing else - in particular not the timestamp, not the sequence number and not the actor' — so I built a two-event ledger, edited `actor` and `ts` in place, and `fsck.check` returned findings=[] , while the positive control on the same harness (same ledger, payload edited in place) returned findings=['unminted-id']; the probe discriminates, so the empty result is a real miss and not a bad probe. Second, `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/fsck.py:176-177` states the limit itself: 'It catches an edit, not a forger - a rewrite that re-minted the id too reads as an ordinary append', which is exactly what `scrub_ledger` does. The only supporting test, tests/test_kit_tracker_events.py::test_fsck_reports_a_withdrawn_log_sound_and_a_hand_edited_one_broken, mutates `payload` alone at line 1841, so nothing exercises the non-digested-field or re-minting-rewriter cases the sentence promises.

payload.title: edge adoption made the differential reference a derivative of the owned ledger

payload.name: description
payload.value:
## Steps to Reproduce

Measured 2026-08-16, immediately after `basicly-vkh0.32` landed as `e69a61b`.

    uv run basicly tracker shadow
    35 record(s) in scope, 9 of them adopted; 866 imported, 0 declared
      refused: Refusal(rule='derived-from-owned-ledger', detail="the reference's answers
      moved when one synthetic event was added to the owned ledger, so it is a function of
      that ledger rather than an independent source")
    clean: no · conclusive: yes

Earlier the same day, before that landing, the same command reported two disagreements and NO refusal:

    31 record(s) in scope, 9 of them adopted; 866 imported, 0 declared
      disagreement: record=basicly-vkh0.27, query=ready, owned=True, reference=False
      disagreement: record=basicly-vkh0.29, query=ready, owned=True, reference=False
    clean: no · conclusive: yes

## Why this is not a false positive

The audit is a perturbation probe. It appends one synthetic status event to the event set the reference is handed and refuses a reference whose answers move with it. The kit's own module docstring states the discriminator:

    A genuinely live source ignores the argument, so it cannot false-fire.

The reference moved. By the audit's own construction that means the reference is now reading the owned ledger rather than being independent of it.

## Why it matters more than the two disagreements it replaced

The differential is the instrument that licenses the flip. A refusal is worse than a disagreement: a disagreement names two records to fix, while a refusal says the comparison cannot discriminate at all. Step 4 of the cutover waits on a clean AND conclusive run, and a refused reference can never produce one.

The work that caused it is the work that was meant to remove the last blocker. That inversion is the finding.

## Where to look, not yet established

`edge_adoption.shortfall` is pure by construction - its own docstring says nothing there loads a kit, reads a file or runs a process, and the kit modules arrive as parameters. It is called from `br.py:1499` on the adoption path, not the read path. So the module import alone does not explain it, and the mechanism has NOT been traced.

Two candidates, neither confirmed:

1. The reference callable the differential builds now threads ledger events into a path that reaches a br view.
2. Adoption changed the reference's own inputs, so the perturbation reaches it indirectly.

Do not assume either. Trace the reference callable the differential constructs and find which argument now carries ledger events.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the shadow differential runs when the reference is audited then the reference is independent of the owned ledger and the run reports no refusal
- Given a reference that genuinely derives from the owned ledger then the refusal still fires, proven by a deliberate derivative as a positive control

## Scope

- `src/basicly/tracker_cutover.py`
- `src/basicly/br.py`
- `tests/test_tracker_cutover.py`

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a repo that discovers work belonging to another repo when it announces an offer in the development exchange then no write reaches the target repo's tracker, and given the target repo polls and pulls the offer then it creates its own bead recording the offer id and appends a claimed event to the exchange so a double pull is detectable
payload.description:
## Context

Settled by the owner 2026-07-25. Several repos are worked at once and work is routinely discovered in the wrong repo - a basicly bug surfaces while working in terminal. The resolution is Kanban pull semantics: announce, never push.

Each repo's ledger has exactly one writer, that repo. The development workspace hosts an exchange - an append-only log of offers rather than assignments. A repo that finds foreign work announces an event naming the target repo; it does not create a bead there. Design work brainstormed in development is decomposed in development and its children announced the same way, so the exchange is the single place work becomes available. Consumers poll at their own cadence, pull by creating a bead in their own tracker recording the offer id as provenance, and append the claim back to the exchange rather than to another tracker.

Event kinds are append-only and total - announced, claimed, declined, superseded - so an offer's state is a fold over its events and history is the audit trail. The design consequence worth preserving: an announcement carries no authority, which is the engine-disposes agents-propose stance applied across repo boundaries, and it is what keeps concurrency trivial since no component ever writes across a repo boundary.

This bead covers the design and the schema in docs/work-tracker.md section 8 plus the exchange format; the commands that announce, poll and pull follow once the format is settled.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a repo that discovers work belonging to another repo when it announces an offer in the development exchange then no write reaches the target repo's tracker, and given the target repo polls and pulls the offer then it creates its own bead recording the offer id and appends a claimed event to the exchange so a double pull is detectable

## Scope

- `docs/work-tracker.md`

payload.description:
basicly loop preflight prints an advisory every pass: no append-only path declared, a path every lane writes is invisible to the grouping until it is listed. The path is .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl - every lane writes tracker events, they mirror into the owned ledger, and the ledger is committed.

Declaring it in [worktree] append_only_paths is the wrong remedy. That list is empty on purpose: its own comment records that CHANGELOG.md was the whole list and that serializing every lane was the cost of detecting a collision the repo created for itself. decompose serializes every child that does not declare the path and call it shared, and no bead declares it, so declaring it today serializes every plan.

basicly-4746 is the precedent: it removed the cause rather than describing it, by giving each lane its own changelog.d fragment file that basicly release assembles. The ledger already has the same shape available - events.LOG_GLOB folds every events-*.jsonl, snapshot.rotate exists and has no caller, and the lexicographic ordering rule is written down. A per-lane segment would make the log a set of files no two lanes share, so nothing contends and the advisory disappears because the fact behind it is gone.

Open question the build must answer: whether a segment is per lane or per period, and how a segment name sorts against the year-period rotation names the kit already reserves.

payload.description:
## Context

Deleting the external store today would destroy the body of nine records, four of them the cutover's own beads. The differential does not see it, and reports clean.

Measured 2026-08-17 over `.basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl` and `.beads/issues.jsonl`. Both stores hold **910 records**. The owned ledger holds a `created` event for **901** of them. The nine without one:

    basicly-e2mz.20   comment, edge, status
    basicly-e2mz.21   comment, edge, status
    basicly-u2hl.55   comment, edge, status
    basicly-u2hl.56   comment, edge, status
    basicly-vkh0.25   comment, edge, status
    basicly-vkh0.26   comment, edge, field, gate, status
    basicly-vkh0.27   comment, edge, field, gate, status
    basicly-vkh0.28   comment, edge, field, gate, status
    basicly-vkh0.29   comment, edge, field

The `created` event is the only carrier of a record's title, description, type, priority and acceptance criteria. For these nine the owned store holds the work log, the status, the edges and the gates, and nothing that says what the work was.

The arithmetic points at the cause. The import took 866 records. 910 minus 866 is 44 created after it, of which 35 have a mirrored `created` event and nine do not. So the nine were created in the window before the mirror covered the `create` surface, or by a direct spawn that never entered the mirror at all.

## Why the differential says clean anyway

`differential.QUERIES` is `(phase, ready, gates)`. Three derived answers, and not one of them reads a record's body. So a clean and conclusive verdict is a statement about three queries agreeing, not about the owned store being able to reproduce a record. The verdict is not wrong; it is narrower than the sentence a reader takes from it, and the gap is exactly the data the flip is supposed to make safe to delete.

## Why this blocks the deletion rather than the flip

The flip changes which store answers. Deleting the external store removes the only copy of these nine bodies. So this is a precondition of the deletion and of the fresh-consumer criterion, not of the mode change.

One ordering trap sits behind it: the import path deliberately refuses a ledger that already holds records created after the import, so a reconciling re-import cannot simply be run later. Whatever backfills these nine has to be either a corrective append per record or a widened import that is allowed to run on a live ledger, and that choice is the design question here.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/tracker_cutover.py`
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/differential.py`
- `tests/test_tracker_cutover.py`
- `tests/test_kit_tracker_differential.py`
payload.title: nine records have no body in the owned ledger and the differential cannot see it

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:
Given every record the external store holds then the owned ledger holds a created event for it, carrying the title description type and priority
Given a record whose body the owned ledger lacks then a check names it and exits non-zero, so the gap cannot be discovered by deleting the store
Given the differential then it compares a record body as well as phase ready and gates, or it says in its own output which fields it does not compare
Given the nine records named in this bead then each has a body in the owned ledger and a fresh consumer reading only the ledger can print it
Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_tracker_cutover.py tests/test_kit_tracker_differential.py -q

payload.text:
Detection landed 2026-08-17 in a99859f. Backfill designed, proven on a copy, and blocked on one line in another bead's file.

## What landed

`.scripts/ledger_bodies.py` names every record the ledger holds no `created` event for and exits 1, with six tests. Against the live ledger:

    ledger-bodies: 9 of 922 record(s) in .basicly/ledger have no body; deleting the
    external store would destroy the only copy

And `basicly tracker shadow` now states what it did not compare:

    not compared: a record's title, description, type, priority or acceptance criteria
    - the three queries read its status, comments, edges and gate rows only, so a clean
    verdict does not say the owned ledger can reproduce a record

## Why a check beside the differential rather than a fourth query

Three reasons, and the third is decisive. A body query needs `br._live_views` to populate body fields, and that module belonged to a live lane. Comparing body *content* across the stores would manufacture disagreements, because the committed export is redacted and the live tracker is not — while the defect here is **presence**, answerable from the owned ledger alone. And `differential.py` has **zero** size headroom, 10950 of 10950 frozen, as does its test module at 7212 of 7212, so any addition fails `module-size` and the honest remedies are an extraction or a waiver, both their own track.

## The backfill: mechanism chosen, proven, and one line short

`migrate._plan_record` already appends a `created` event whenever `held.created is None`, so **no relaxation of the import refusal is needed** — and relaxing it was rejected outright, because `import_preview.native`'s refusal exists to stop the historical gap being closed by re-import and would absorb genuine dual-write failures into history.

The gap is purely selection, in `br.adopt_hand_writes`:

    undeclared = {ids} - {records in the ledger} - {baseline records}
    wanted = undeclared | held

A bodyless record is in the ledger's record set, so it is subtracted out of `undeclared`; it has no `created` event, so it is not in `held`. It falls in neither set. The fix is `wanted = undeclared | held | bodyless`.

Proven on a copy under /tmp, never the real ledger: 9 bodyless before, 0 after; 5485 lines before, 5595 after; every original line unchanged and in place; each backfilled record arrives with its title, type, priority, description and acceptance criteria under `hand-write-adoption`.

**Blocked:** that line lives in `src/basicly/br.py`, which `basicly-wpc8.1` was holding. Apply it once that lane has landed.

## Two things deliberately not done

**The check is not wired to a `[[verify.checks]]` entry, on purpose.** Nine records are bodyless today, so a wired gate would exit 1 on every commit in this repository. Wire it in the same change that lands the backfill, as a `basicly.d/basicly-vkh0.41.toml` drop-in — the mechanism `basicly-vkh0.37` proved works.

**`basicly tracker shadow` still prints `clean: yes` over the nine.** `br.scoped_differential` wraps the report in `baseline.scope`, which builds a fixed-field `ScopedReport` reading only `disagreements`, `unknown` and `refusals`, so any new finding field on `DifferentialReport` is dropped before the command sees it. Surfacing body presence through that command needs `baseline.py` plus a seam function. The natural home is `fsck.py`, which already owns severities and exit codes for ledger defects.

payload.text:
Landed in 5d109d0 as session work, not a lane, per the below-floor sizing on the bead.

What changed. The gate resolves its id set from the owned ledger first and the external export second, and reports which file it read. An empty store counts as no source rather than as an empty id set, so a store that exists and holds nothing falls through instead of refusing every commit. The tracker root is resolved once, following the redirect, and both stores hang off it, so the ledger obeys the same one-store-per-repository rule the export does.

Exercised as the gate runs, not only in tests. With a known id: exit 0, "Issue id reference is valid." With an unknown id: exit 1, and the message names `.basicly/ledger/events-*.jsonl` as the file it checked, which is the proof the source switched.

Gates: 4293 passed in the full suite, verify --mode fast PASS, ruff clean.

One deviation from the second acceptance criterion, stated rather than hidden. It asked that the refusal carry no reference to the deleted directory. The message names the file it actually read, so on the fallback path it does name the export. That path exists only while the export is the sole store, which is the case for a consumer before the cutover, and naming a file the reader can open is worth more than a message that hides which store answered.

Two traps this hit, both worth the next reader's time. The kit owns the log glob as events.LOG_GLOB and a hook may not reach into the kit, so the hook carries its own spelling and a test now pins the two together - a drifting glob matches nothing, reads the ledger as empty, and would fail open onto a store that is about to be deleted. And loading a kit module through spec_from_file_location without registering it in sys.modules first raises inside dataclasses on the first decorated class, because a dataclass resolves its annotations through sys.modules[cls.__module__].

Wording changed in two places outside the hook: tests/test_git_hooks/test_beads_commit_msg.py and tests/test_kit_tracker_ids.py:486, the second of which is a positive control in another module that asserted the old message text. The whole suite found it; the hook's own tests did not.

## What the residue sweep found

A whole-tree probe over tracked files (2026-08-18) for the binary, the store directory and
the export filename. The probe:
`(^|[^a-zA-Z<._-])(br|bv)([ .]exe|\s+[a-z][a-z-]+)`, `\.beads`, `\bbeads\b`, `issues\.jsonl`.
Positive control: the probe returns 5130 hits in the ledger, so a zero elsewhere is a real
zero.

| Population | Files | Hits | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `.basicly/ledger/` | 1 | 5130 | keep — the history is the record |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | 1 | 102 | keep — a released entry describes what shipped then |
| `tests/` | 66 | 282 | prose in fixtures and rationale; low value |
| engine `src/` | 34 | 206 | prose; three false claims already fixed |
| `docs/` | 4 | 62 | basicly-vkh0.42.6 owns these |
| **`.basicly/core/kit/`** | **8** | **25** | **this record** |

## Why the kit is the one that matters

The kit ships to a consumer by copy. A repository that installs it gets
`differential.py` explaining its own row shape in terms of `br gate list`, `scheduler.py`
citing `br schema issue` for the priority default, `migrate.py` describing `.beads/issues.jsonl`
as "the export the current tracker already writes" — a tracker the consumer has never had.
Every other population above is read only by people working in *this* repository, who have
the history. The kit's readers do not.

`migrate.py` is the exception to check rather than rewrite: it genuinely reads a foreign
export in that format, so its references are a live input contract, not a stale citation.
Establish which before editing it.

## Already fixed under basicly-vkh0.42, not part of this

Three user-facing false claims, found by the same sweep:
`commit.py` told the user to run `br sync --flush-only` against an `issues.jsonl` that no
longer exists; `cli.py`'s `policy dor` help said "via br lint"; `policy.py`'s module
docstring said the same and contradicted its own line 177.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the kit sources when the probe above is run then every remaining hit is a live
  input contract of `migrate.py`, and each is named in that module's docstring as one
- Given `kit-boundary` and the kit CLI's own walk when they run then both still pass
- Given a consumer reading a kit module cold when it cites a behaviour then that behaviour
  is one the kit itself has

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/`

## Context

Owner decision 2026-08-19. `docs/requirements/` is **not** deleted. A long-lived design branch was refused, and a ledger event was refused as the home for a 1178-line design. The folder stays as the place a requirement is born, and every requirement created there from now on carries **one identifiable structure** an agent, a skill and a script can each act on.

This **amends** the v1.0.0 rule `basicly-vkh0.42.6` cites. The rule now reads: a requirements document that describes **shipped** work is absorbed into the architecture and deleted; a document that states work **not yet built** lives in `docs/requirements/` in the register form until its acceptance criteria close.

## What is missing

Nothing structures or identifies a requirement document today. The two that exist are 1568 and 1585 lines of mixed claim, decision and measurement, with no shared section set, no id and no gate. The marker roster and requirement register read `architecture.md` after basicly-vkh0.42.8, not this folder, so a malformed requirement is invisible to every gate.

The six machine-checked sections architecture section 33 already specifies for `solution-design` are the obvious candidate format rather than a new invention.

## Acceptance Criteria

Given a new requirement document then it carries a machine-checkable section set and a record id that resolves in the tracker.
Given a requirement document whose sections do not conform then a verify check fails and names the missing section.
Given an author asks for a new requirement then a scaffold command writes the conforming skeleton rather than the author copying an existing file.
Given every acceptance criterion a requirement carries is closed then a check reports the document as absorbable rather than deleting it.
Given the folder holds no requirement document then no gate changes behaviour.
Demonstrated by: uv run basicly verify --mode fast with a deliberately malformed requirement present, showing the check fail and then pass once corrected

## Open question the owner left open

Whether an implemented requirement is deleted or kept forever. The owner said whichever is better. A recommendation is recorded as a comment on this record.

- `.basicly/core/`
- `.scripts/`
- `src/basicly/`
- `docs/requirements/`

## Context

`basicly-vkh0.42.6` landed the architecture half in commit c32b23dd: section 37 is now a closing account of a dependency that already left, and five further claims that outlived the removal were corrected. **It deliberately did not delete the document**, because doing so strands the citations, and repairing them needed files outside its declared scope.

This record is the deletion and the repair.

## The measured citation blast radius, 2026-08-19

A tree search finds the filename in **29 files**. Notably **all thirteen tracker kit modules** cite it, which is the largest single population: baseline, cli, commands, differential, events, fsck, ids, migrate, provenance, queries, scheduler, snapshot, plus the kit boundary hook.

Beyond the kit: the board snapshot schema, the configuration file, the project file, three engine modules being owned store and tracker and verify, five tests, the architecture document, the implementation plan, the sibling requirements document and a research document. Plus the shipped release notes.

## Three populations, and only the first is work

**Repoint** a citation standing in for a rule the architecture now carries. The kit modules are this population, and the kit is a standalone consumable, so a citation pointing at a document the consumer never receives is a defect in the kit independent of this deletion.

**Keep** a citation that is dated history. The shipped release notes name it and are correct as they stand. `tests/test_tracker_requirements.py` keeps the name deliberately as dated history and is correct too.

**Delete** a citation that only pointed at prose the absorption drops.

Do not treat a residue count as a defect count. Name the expected count per population before editing and reconcile after. A whole tree replace that does not split by population first is how a previous sweep left four false user facing messages in the tree.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the document is deleted when the gates run then none reports a dangling reference and the verify pipeline is green.
- Given a kit module that cited the document when a consumer installs the kit alone then its citation names something the consumer can reach.
- Given a citation that is dated history when the sweep runs then it is left alone and the record says which ones those are.
- Given the counts when the work completes then the record states the expected and actual count per population and they agree.
- Given a claim in the document that merely restates shipped code when the absorption runs then it is dropped rather than relocated.

## Scope

payload.text: [scope exclusion, deliberate] Four files that cite the document are held out of this record scope because live lanes claim them: the kit events module and the kit migrate module and the engine tracker module and the kit provenance test. basicly-u2hl.60 and basicly-u2hl.61 own two of them. So this record repoints nine of the thirteen kit modules and leaves four citations standing. That is a declared partial, not an oversight: state the four in the change summary and file the remainder rather than widening into a running lane. Expected count after this record: four residual citations in those four files, all in the repoint population.

[re-measured 2026-08-19, and the work is much larger than the file count implied] The 29 file count undercounts the real dependency. The kit does not cite the document by name in each place; it names it once per module header and then uses BARE section references throughout. Measured: 127 bare section references inside .basicly/core/kit/, and the events module header line 4 names work-tracker.md section 4 explicitly before using section 4.1, section 15 and section 4.6 as bare pointers. Named citations across the whole tree are only 36: 25 name the architecture, 10 name factory-loop.md, 1 names work-tracker.md. There are 233 further bare section references outside the kit. SO THE SHAPE OF THIS RECORD CHANGES. It is not a repoint of thirteen module headers. Deleting the document orphans 127 bare pointers in a standalone consumable, and a consumer installing the kit alone already receives 127 references to a document that was never shipped to them. That is a defect in the kit today, before any deletion. Three options and this record does not choose: absorb the cited sections into the kit own module prose so the kit is self contained, which is the only option that fixes the consumer case; or repoint every bare reference at an architecture section, which keeps the dependency and moves it; or give the kit its own short specification that ships with it. Whichever is chosen, name the expected count per population first and reconcile after, because 127 plus 233 residue hits read as one number is how a previous sweep left four false user facing messages in the tree.

[owner-decision 2026-08-20] The record named three options for the 127 bare section references inside the kit and chose none. DECIDED: give the kit its own specification that ships with it. It fixes the consumer defect that exists today, a kit only install receiving references to a document never shipped to it, and it keeps the references resolvable by shipping their target rather than rewriting 360 of them. Rejected: absorbing the cited sections into module prose, because it duplicates one source into thirteen copies and the comment density ratchet is already at its cap. Rejected: repointing every bare reference at architecture.md, because a kit only install still cannot read that file so the consumer defect survives the largest sweep. Method that still binds: name the expected count per population first and reconcile after.

payload.description:
## The defect

`basicly loop preflight` prints a remediation line instructing the operator to run a command that cannot run. `src/basicly/cli.py` line 2931:

```
print(f"           cover each: br dep add {state.root_issue} <id> -t blocks")
```

The binary is gone from every checkout, so this is a consumer facing instruction that fails whoever follows it. Five more surfaces carry the same name in text a consumer reads, all in the same module: the verify help at 4402 and 4415, the decompose help at 4462, the scaffold help at 4535, the classify help at 4651.

`basicly-e2mz.44` is closed and covered a different thing, the seam **argument grammar** that a human types. This is the engine printing the retired name back at the operator.

## The population, and why a raw count is the wrong instrument

A search for the binary name across the engine and the catalog returns 122 hits and **the overwhelming majority are docstring prose**, which is history and correctly left alone. Only text a consumer reads is a defect: a printed line, a help string, an error message. Split the population before editing, name the expected count per population, and reconcile after. A sweep that treated 122 as a defect count is how a previous removal left four false user facing messages in the tree.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `basicly loop preflight` on a root whose blockers are not all covered, so the remediation branch is reached.
2. Read the printed line. Observe it instructs a `dep add` through the retired binary.
3. Run that instruction. Observe the binary is not on PATH.
4. Run `basicly loop preflight --help`, `basicly verify --help`, `basicly decompose --help`, `basicly policy scaffold --help` and `basicly loop run --help`. Observe five help strings naming the binary.
5. Positive control for the population split: the same search finds the name in docstrings, and those are history rather than defects, so a raw count over the tree does not answer this.

Observed: the engine prints an instruction naming a tool no checkout has, and five help strings do the same.
Expected: text a consumer reads names a command the consumer can run.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the preflight remediation branch when it prints then the instruction names a command that exists on the current checkout.
- Given every help string in the command line surface when it is read then none names the retired binary.
- Given a docstring naming the binary as history when the sweep runs then it is left alone, and the record states how many were left and why.
- Given the counts when the work completes then the expected and actual count per population agree, and the record states both.
- Given a gate for this when it runs then it binds on printed and help text rather than on a raw tree search, because a raw search cannot tell prose from a message.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_cli.py`

Partly landed 2026-08-17. Both binary installs are deleted: quality-gates.yml and improvement-loop.yml.

The path filter is not landed, and the reason is a three-place contract. tests/test_cli.py asserts exact equality of the ignore list against three sources at once: basicly.yml, quality-gates.yml and scaffolds.CONSUMER_CI_WORKFLOW. Any edit to one turns that test red and cannot be fixed inside the workflows. Landing it takes one commit touching scaffolds.py, tests/test_cli.py and both workflows together.

payload.description:
## Context

Two committed and pushed files carry a person's username and a personal e-mail address. Architecture §32.7 claimed absolutely that no committed artifact carries a username, and the claim is false.

Measured 2026-08-17, twice by paths sharing no step — a field-wise count over the parsed records and a raw-line regex over the bytes — and both agree on the substance:

    .beads/issues.jsonl, 924 records
      created_by: <redacted:machine-username> 846, <redacted:machine-username> 78
      assignee:   <redacted:email> 56, <redacted:machine-username> 26
      lines holding an e-mail address: 58

    .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl, 5616 lines
      lines holding an e-mail address: 59
      lines holding the redaction placeholder: 4944   <- positive control, the rule does fire

Both files are tracked, committed and pushed to a public remote, so this is published rather than merely present.

## Why every gate is green over it

`tracker-path-scan` builds its identity rule from `getpass.getuser()`, which on this machine is `<redacted:machine-username>`. The identity in the stores is a **different** one. So the gate is not broken and its green result is correct — it is answering "does this artifact carry *your* identity" when the requirement is "does it carry *anyone's*".

That is the general defect, and it is worth stating separately from the data: an identity gate keyed on the running user cannot see another user's identity, and a repository that several machines write to will accumulate identities no single machine's gate can find.

## What is bounded and what is not

Every identity-bearing event in the owned ledger carries the import's own source marker; no live write path produces one. So the population is inherited from the pre-cutover import and is not growing. That bounds the remedy to a backfill plus a format rule — it does not make the published values unpublished.

## The three remedies, and which needs an owner

Removing the values from the current files is a corrective append or a rewrite, and the rewrite of a committed append-only log is the exception architecture §4.2 reserves for an explicit owner decision. Removing them from **history** is a force-push, which is an owner decision of a different order and is not this bead's to take. Preventing the next one is the format rule and the deny-list configuration, which is ordinary work.

Note the deny-list the hook already names, `[[privacy.denied]]`, belongs in the gitignored `basicly.local.toml` — 787 bytes, all comments, parsing to an empty table. The mechanism exists and was never configured.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/migrate.py`
- `src/basicly/redact.py`
- `.basicly/core/hooks/tracker-path-scan.py`
- `.basicly/core/hooks/internal-info-scan.py`
- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`
- `docs/architecture/status.md`
- `tests/test_br_scrub_ledger.py`

payload.text:
Correcting my own framing on this bead, which I filed at p0 as a published-identity exposure.

There is no disclosure. `git log --format="%an <%ae>" | sort -u` returns exactly one identity for the whole repository: <redacted:git-user-name> <<redacted:email>>. That address is the commit author on every commit here, so git published it on every object long before the tracker carried it in an assignee field. The 56 assignee values add no exposure at all.

What remains is the username `<redacted:machine-username>`, in exactly two files and nowhere else in the tree, across 69 commits. It is a username with no credential value and no link to anything. No token, no secret.

So the remedy is a corrective append and nothing more. A history rewrite is off the table - I raised it, and I should not have, because I inferred exposure from an identity being present in a committed file without first measuring what the repository already publishes. The old blobs contain nothing that is not already in every commit header.

The defect is real but it is format consistency rather than disclosure. Architecture section 32.7 claims absolutely that no committed artifact carries a username, and 78 of 924 export records carry a bare one against 846 carrying the placeholder, so the claim is false. The general shape is what matters: tracker-path-scan builds its rule from getpass.getuser(), so it catches this machine identity and can never catch another, and a repository several machines write to accumulates identities no single machine gate can see.

Re-graded from 0 to 2 and the acceptance criterion about an owner decision on rewriting history is withdrawn.

Both files are tracked, committed and pushed to a public remote, so this is published rather than merely present.

## Why every gate is green over it

`tracker-path-scan` builds its identity rule from `getpass.getuser()`, which on this machine is `<redacted:machine-username>`. The identity in the stores is a **different** one. So the gate is not broken and its green result is correct — it is answering "does this artifact carry *your* identity" when the requirement is "does it carry *anyone's*".

That is the general defect, and it is worth stating separately from the data: an identity gate keyed on the running user cannot see another user's identity, and a repository that several machines write to will accumulate identities no single machine's gate can find.

## What is bounded and what is not

Every identity-bearing event in the owned ledger carries the import's own source marker; no live write path produces one. So the population is inherited from the pre-cutover import and is not growing. That bounds the remedy to a backfill plus a format rule — it does not make the published values unpublished.

## The three remedies, and which needs an owner

Removing the values from the current files is a corrective append or a rewrite, and the rewrite of a committed append-only log is the exception architecture §4.2 reserves for an explicit owner decision. Removing them from **history** is a force-push, which is an owner decision of a different order and is not this bead's to take. Preventing the next one is the format rule and the deny-list configuration, which is ordinary work.

Note the deny-list the hook already names, `[[privacy.denied]]`, belongs in the gitignored `basicly.local.toml` — 787 bytes, all comments, parsing to an empty table. The mechanism exists and was never configured.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Count the identity-bearing lines in the committed store, with the redaction placeholder
   as the control that proves the rule fires at all:

       git grep -c -E '[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}' HEAD -- .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl
       git grep -c '<redacted:machine-username>' HEAD -- .
       grep -c 'redacted:' .basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl

2. Run the gate that is supposed to catch this and read its result:

       uv run pre-commit run tracker-path-scan --all-files

3. Read why that result is green, which is the general defect:

       rg -n 'getpass|getuser' .basicly/core/hooks/tracker-path-scan.py

4. Check whether the deny-list the hooks already name was ever configured:

       rg -n 'privacy.denied' basicly.local.toml
       wc -c basicly.local.toml
       rg -n 'privacy.*denied' .basicly/core/hooks/internal-info-scan.py

   Observed 2026-08-19: the first command returns nothing, `basicly.local.toml` is **787
   bytes and every line of it is a comment**, and the third command is the **positive
   control** - `internal-info-scan.py` reads `data.get("privacy", {}).get("denied", [])`
   out of exactly that file, and `tracker-path-scan.py` names the same list. So the
   mechanism exists, reads this file, and was never configured; the empty result is a
   missing configuration rather than a missing feature.

Observed, re-measured 2026-08-19 in this checkout: the ledger holds 6027 lines, **61** of
them carrying an e-mail address and **213** carrying the username `<redacted:machine-username>`, and `git grep`
finds `<redacted:machine-username>` in that one file and nowhere else in the tree - so the values are committed
at HEAD, not merely present in a working copy. **The positive control is the third command**,
which returns **4955** lines carrying the redaction placeholder: the rule does fire, over the
same bytes, on the great majority of records. So the 61 and the 213 are a population the rule
missed rather than a probe that failed.

Step 3 shows why: `tracker-path-scan` builds its identity rule from `getpass.getuser()`, so
it asks "does this artifact carry *your* identity" where the requirement is "does it carry
*anyone's*". The gate is not broken and its green result is correct - the rule is the wrong
question. An identity gate keyed on the running user cannot see another user's identity, and
a repository several machines write to accumulates identities no single machine's gate can
find.

**One of the two stores this record was filed over is gone.** `.beads/issues.jsonl` and its
924 records are no longer in the tree or in git's index - `git ls-files .beads` returns
nothing - so the 846/78 `created_by` and 56/26 `assignee` counts in the Context above are
history rather than a current reading, and `docs/architecture` §32.7.1 ("two stores carry
another") is itself now one store out of date. The owned ledger half above stands and is the
live population.

Expected: the format rule refuses an identity-bearing field on the write path whoever the
running user is; the inherited values are removed from the current file by the corrective
route architecture §4.2 reserves for an append-only log; and the architecture claim is
restated to match what is measurable.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/migrate.py`
- `src/basicly/redact.py`
- `.basicly/core/hooks/tracker-path-scan.py`
- `.basicly/core/hooks/internal-info-scan.py`
- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`
- `docs/architecture/status.md`
- `tests/test_br_scrub_ledger.py`

payload.description:
## Context

Found during the work-tracker review 2026-07-25. The committed .beads/issues.jsonl carries source_repo_path on 328 of its 332 records, and the values expose two different users' home directories - <redacted:posix-absolute-path><user-a><redacted:posix-absolute-path> and <redacted:posix-absolute-path><user-b><redacted:posix-absolute-path> - plus a transient worktree path under .claude/worktrees. The file is committed and this repo is distributed to consumers, so the leak is published.

This violates the repo's own hard constraint that no machine or user specific absolute path, username or hostname may ever be committed. It is also a portability defect in its own right: a path that means something on one machine is noise or a wrong answer on another, and a consumer's clone inherits our directory layout as data.

The field is written by br rather than by the harness, so the fix is either to strip it on export, to configure br not to emit it if that is possible, or to add a gate that catches an absolute path in the tracker export the way secret-scan catches a credential. Whichever route, the requirement for our own tracker is recorded in docs/work-tracker.md: a record is path-free, and provenance is the repo identity rather than a filesystem location.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `grep -c "<redacted:posix-absolute-path>" .beads/issues.jsonl` in a clean checkout.
2. It reports hundreds of matches.
3. Inspect one record with `head -1 .beads/issues.jsonl | jq .source_repo_path` and observe an absolute path containing a username.

Expected: no absolute path or username appears anywhere in the committed export.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the committed tracker export when it is scanned then no record carries a machine-specific absolute path or username, and the harness either strips the field on write or fails the secret-scan style gate that catches it

## Scope

- `src/basicly/br.py`
- `.basicly/core/hooks/`

payload.description:
## The defect

`tracker_write.py` lines 40 and 41 call `tracker.write(...)` and then print `recorded: <argv>` **unconditionally**. Nothing checks that an event was appended. So a dropped write and a landed write print the same line and both exit zero, and the caller cannot tell them apart.

This is the fail-open shape: a write surface whose success message is not evidence of success.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a loop lane so the ledger is being written concurrently, for example `basicly loop run <some-record> --autonomy L3` in the background.
2. While it runs, issue `basicly tracker write -- update <record> --notes "probe"`.
3. Observe `recorded: update <record> --notes probe` and exit zero.
4. Count the events on that record. Observe no `field` event.
5. Wait for the lane to finish, then repeat step 2.
6. Observe the same success line, and this time a `field` event with `name=notes` appears, and the ledger line count rises by one.

Observed, measured 2026-08-19: three consecutive update invocations printed `recorded:` and appended nothing, then a fourth identical in form appended one event. The committed file held 5854 lines and the working tree held 5855 after the fourth, so **no reset discarded the first three** — they never appended.

Expected: a write that does not append says so and exits non zero.

## What is established and what is not

**Established.** The translation is correct: `mirror.drafts` returns exactly one `field` draft for an update, verified in isolation. The append is correct: called directly against a copy of the ledger it grew the log from 5854 to 5855 and returned the event. `classify_access` calls `update` a write, so the empty-drafts branch in `mirror.drafts` is not the cause. The success message is printed with no reference to the result.

**Not established.** Why the three writes were dropped. Candidates, none confirmed: a read only section active during a lane landing, which is designed to refuse a write at the seam and should raise rather than pass; a ledger lock timeout, which raises a ledger error the seam converts and should also surface; or a third path. The record deliberately does not guess.

## Why it matters more than it looks

The ledger has no undo, so a write that vanishes cannot be detected later by reading the log; there is nothing to find. The only place the loss is visible is at the moment of the write, and that is exactly where the surface says the opposite.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a write that appends no event when the seam returns then the command exits non zero and names the record and the flag that did not land.
- Given a write that appends then the message states what it appended rather than echoing the argv.
- Given a write refused by a read only section then the refusal reaches the caller as a refusal rather than as a success line.
- Given a write that cannot take the ledger lock then the caller learns it was not recorded and may retry.
- Given a concurrent lane holding the lock when a write is issued then the outcome is one of appended or explicitly refused, never silently neither.
- Given the existing passing tests then they still pass.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/tracker_write.py`
- `src/basicly/tracker.py`
- `src/basicly/owned_write.py`
- `tests/`
payload.title: the tracker write seam reports recorded whether or not the write landed

payload.text: [sharpened reproduction 2026-08-19, and the hypotheses already killed so the lane does not repeat them] THE CORRELATION IS CONCURRENCY. A write through the seam lands when no loop lane is running and is silently dropped when one is. Measured: twenty consecutive update writes issued while lanes ran produced zero events; the same twenty issued in a quiet tree all landed on the first attempt, reconciled from twenty near misses to zero. Earlier the same day, three update writes were dropped while a lane ran and a fourth landed once the lane finished. ALREADY RULED OUT, with the check: the argv translation is correct, mirror.drafts returns exactly one field draft for an update; the append is correct, called directly against a copy of the ledger it grew the log by one and returned the event; classify_access calls update a write so the empty drafts branch in mirror.drafts is not reached; LedgerLock.__exit__ returns None so it does not swallow the exception; LedgerLock.acquire raises LockUnavailableError on timeout and on exceeding the steal bound, so it is not fail open. What remains unexamined is the path between owned_write.append taking the lock and events.append returning, under contention. A WARNING FOR WHOEVER VERIFIES THIS: a ledger line count delta is NOT a valid instrument under concurrency. It gave me a false positive, reporting delta equals one for a write that never landed, because a concurrent lane appended a line in the same window. It also read 834 and minus 1 in single windows. Verify by reading the folded field back and comparing content, and note that even a fold can race, because a reader takes no lock and can observe a partial final line.

[ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-19 - tests/conftest.py line 244] The write is not dropped by the write path. It is REVERTED by the test suite. The autouse fixture _the_live_ledger_is_never_written reads the bytes of every events-NNNN.jsonl under the real committed ledger before each test, and after each test, if the bytes changed, it calls path.write_bytes(held) to restore them and then fails the test. LIVE_LEDGER is REPO_ROOT/.basicly/ledger, the actual store, not a temporary one. So any tracker write issued while pytest runs in the base checkout is undone by whichever test happens to be in flight, and the failure is attributed to that innocent test rather than to the writer. This explains every observation exactly: writes vanish while a lane runs, because a lane runs verify which runs pytest in base; writes land in a quiet tree; and a different test was the victim on each of six observed runs while the count stayed at 4216 passed. A worktree lane is immune, because its ledger is a redirect file rather than a directory of event logs, so the glob finds nothing and the guard is inert there. THE SHARP POINT: the fixture docstring describes the original incident as four events landing in an append-only log where the repair was an edit to a file that is supposed to have none. The guard now performs exactly that edit, automatically, on every test, against any concurrent writer. A guard that repairs an append-only log by overwriting it is doing the thing it exists to prevent. RECOMMENDED SHAPE: the guard fails and reports, and never writes. Detection is the valuable half and it is sound. If the revert is kept it must first prove the change was the test and not another process, and it must take the ledger lock, because right now it races the very seam the lock protects. SECOND CONSEQUENCE for the fan out schedule: a pytest run in the base checkout blocks every tracker write for its whole duration, about 90 seconds, silently. Sequence tracker writes before a base verify, never during.

payload.description:
## The defect

`tests/conftest.py` autouse fixture `_the_live_ledger_is_never_written` reads the bytes of every `events-NNNN.jsonl` under the **real committed ledger** before each test, and after each test, if the bytes changed, it calls `path.write_bytes(held)` to restore them and then fails the test. `LIVE_LEDGER` is `REPO_ROOT/.basicly/ledger`, the actual store.

So any tracker write issued while pytest runs in the base checkout is **undone**, and the failure is attributed to whichever test happened to be in flight rather than to the writer. The writer sees `recorded:` and exit zero, because the seam reports success unconditionally, which is basicly-vkh0.50.

**The fixture docstring describes the original incident as four events landing in an append only log where the repair was an edit to a file that is supposed to have none. The guard now performs exactly that edit, automatically, on every test, against any concurrent writer.** Detection is the sound half. The revert is the defect.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start `uv run pytest -q` in the base checkout.
2. While it runs, issue a tracker write through the seam, for example `basicly tracker write -- update <record> --notes probe`.
3. Observe `recorded:` and exit zero from the write.
4. Read the record back and observe no event.
5. Observe pytest fail on an unrelated test, naming the ledger path, with the total still at its usual passing count.
6. Wait for pytest to finish, then repeat step 2 and observe the event lands.

Observed 2026-08-19: twenty consecutive writes issued while a base agent ran verify produced zero events; the same twenty in a quiet tree landed twenty of twenty on the first attempt. Independently, a lane observed pytest fail on three of six runs with a different victim each time and always 4216 passed.

Expected: the guard fails and reports, and never writes to the store.

## Why the revert cannot simply be kept

The guard races the ledger lock it does not take, so it can overwrite an append that the lock had already serialised. It also cannot tell a test write from another process write, and it currently assumes the former.

## A worktree lane is immune, and that is worth stating

A lane worktree holds a ledger **redirect file** rather than a directory of event logs, so the glob finds nothing and the fixture is inert there. The hazard is specific to an agent running the suite in the base checkout.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a test that writes to the live ledger when the suite runs then the test fails and names the writer, and the ledger is left exactly as the writer left it.
- Given a concurrent process that writes to the live ledger while the suite runs then no test fails on account of it and no byte is restored.
- Given the guard detects a change it cannot attribute to the test then it says so rather than assuming the test.
- Given the original incident shape, a fixture leaving the working directory at the real repository, then the guard still catches it.
- Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_conftest_guard.py -q with a test that appends to the live ledger under a temporary copy, and a second case that appends from another process and is not blamed

## Scope

- `tests/conftest.py`
- `tests/`

evidence.reference: tests/test_conftest_guard.py:99 test_a_test_that_appends_to_the_watched_store_is_named_and_nothing_is_undone — `assert log.read_bytes() == before + PROBE_LINE` after `ledger_guard.report(watch)` raised. tests/test_conftest_guard.py:127 test_a_log_another_process_created_is_reported_and_left_alone — `assert appeared.read_bytes() == PROBE_LINE`; binds the delete branch the old guard had (`path.unlink()`), not only the restore branch.

`rg -n 'write_bytes|write_text|unlink|\.write\(|shutil|os\.remove|rename' tests/ledger_guard.py` → exit 1, no match. The module that owns the reaction contains no mutation call at all. This is the structural form of the claim, independent of the tests.

`uv run pytest -q` on the merged tree → `4225 passed, 1 warning in 99.60s`, exit 0. A concurrent process wrote the real store during that run: `.basicly/ledger/events-0001.jsonl` is 5942 lines against HEAD's 5940 (`wc -l` vs `git show HEAD:...|wc -l`) and still shows ` M` in `git status --short`. Two events survived a full suite run; the old guard would have restored them. Confidence: high — this is the claim demonstrated on the live artifact, not a temp copy.

claims.claim: "a write from the test process fails that test and names it"

evidence.reference: tests/test_conftest_guard.py:99 — `assert NODE in str(blame.value)` and `assert log.name in str(blame.value)`, where NODE is spelled out as a literal at tests/test_conftest_guard.py:30 rather than taken from `request`, so the assertion cannot pass by naming the wrong test.
tests/test_conftest_guard.py:159 test_the_original_incident_shape_still_reaches_the_guard — same blame assertion reached through a real engine write rather than a bare `open`.

tests/test_conftest_guard.py:144 test_reading_the_watched_store_is_not_a_write — the discriminating control. Asserts `watch.written == ()` for a read-only `open`; without it, a hook recording every `open` would pass the two blame tests by attributing the guard's own snapshot read at tests/ledger_guard.py:110.

claims.claim: "a change from another process is reported ... as unattributed" — the second and third acceptance criteria: no test fails on account of it, and it says so rather than assuming the test

evidence.reference: tests/test_conftest_guard.py:105 test_a_write_from_another_process_is_reported_and_not_blamed — asserts `watch.written == ()`, `watch.unexplained == (str(log),)`, exactly one `LedgerChangedWarning`, and the notice text `no write from this process explains it` / `No test is blamed`. No test is blamed for it and no byte was restored.` Suite still `4225 passed`, exit 0. body.post_ship_action: BEFORE THE TAG MOVES (owner's edit; I am read-only and changed nothing): two phrases in changelog.d/basicly-vkh0.51.fixed.md should change, because curating after `basicly release` never publishes — the workflow reads the tagged commit. (1) 'sees every route' → 'sees every in-process route', plus one clause naming the boundary: a test that writes the live ledger from a subprocess it spawns is reported as unattributed, not blamed. (2) The twenty-writes measurement should carry its source ('recorded on basicly-vkh0.51') rather than stand as a repeatable figure. If the owner declines either edit, the release is still honest provided this record ships with it — an unmet criterion documented is fine; one omitted is not. AFTER THE TAG: file two follow-up records under basicly-vkh0 — (a) a test asserting `report` warns once for two changes to the same path, closing the only unsupported behavioural claim; (b) a decision record on whether a subprocess write to the live ledger should fail rather than warn, since that route silently lost its gate in this change. Neither is a blocker for the tag. WHAT I DID NOT INSPECT, so the coverage boundary is not assumed: I did not re-run ruff, pyright, `basicly check`/`skills-check`/`agents-check`/`hooks-check`/`permissions-check`, or the module-size, comment-density and tree-growth ratchets — I took the merged lane's verify/validate green on those and did not re-derive it. I did not read the one-line change to docs/plan/implementation-plan.md. I did not review the other 15 fragments in changelog.d/, only basicly-vkh0.51's, so this record says nothing about the rest of the release's notes. I did not generate or read the assembled CHANGELOG.md, since the tag has not moved. I did not exercise the guard under pytest-xdist or under two concurrent lanes, and I did not measure the audit hook's per-open cost (no claim was made about it). I moved no tag and pushed nothing.

unsupported.claim: "which sees **every route** including a kit loaded by path"

payload.description:
## The defect

`basicly tracker show` reports the same parent-child edge more than once. Measured on `basicly-vkh0`: **65 parent-child rows for 60 unique record ids**, with five ids appearing twice: `basicly-vkh0.25`, `.26`, `.27`, `.28`, `.29`.

So any count read off that surface is inflated, and the inflation is silent. A child count is exactly the kind of number a reader takes at face value: it decides whether an epic looks nearly done, and it feeds a human judgment about whether to close one.

The five duplicated ids are consecutive, which suggests one batch of edge writes was recorded twice rather than five independent accidents. The fold applies each edge event it reads; nothing deduplicates an edge by its endpoints and type.

## Why the append only log is not the problem

The log correctly holds every event it was given. The defect is in the **derived view**: an edge is a relation, so folding two identical edge events must yield one edge. `events.append` already skips a draft whose content derived id is present, so an exact replay is idempotent; what is not deduplicated is two edge events that state the same relation while differing in some other field, for example a provenance label or a timestamp.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `basicly tracker show basicly-vkh0`.
2. Collect the dependents whose type is parent-child and count the rows, then count the distinct ids.
3. Observe 65 rows against 60 distinct ids.
4. Observe the five repeated ids are consecutive.
5. Read the edge events for one repeated id in the ledger and compare their payloads, to establish which field differs.
6. Positive control: do the same on a record with no repeats and observe rows equal distinct ids, so the probe discriminates.

Observed: the derived edge set contains a duplicate relation, and a count taken from it overstates the child set by five.
Expected: two events stating the same relation fold to one edge, and a count off the view equals the count of distinct relations.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given two edge events stating the same source and target and type when the fold runs then the derived view holds one edge.
- Given two such events differing in provenance when they fold then the surviving edge carries the stronger provenance label and the weaker one is not a second row.
- Given the committed ledger when the fold runs then the parent-child row count for every record equals its distinct target count.
- Given the fold before and after the fix when it runs over the committed log then no record loses an edge it previously had.
- Given a record with no duplicate when the fix lands then its view is byte identical to before.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py`
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/provenance.py`
- `tests/test_kit_tracker_events.py`

This is the new one and it is worse than the field. br comments offers only add and list - no edit, no delete - so a machine path (or anything else) recorded in a comment cannot be removed through the documented CLI at all. Two usernames on closed beads were only fixable by redacting at export time, which means the committed artifact deliberately diverges from the local database. Our replacement needs a first-class redaction event: append-only history is right, but an append-only log with no redaction event cannot honour a deletion requirement.

payload.description:
## Context

Found immediately after basicly-vkh0.2 landed, by checking a claim that bead's own report
made: the surface report lists `where` as never used, yet `worktree._probe_redirect` calls
`br where --json` on every single worktree provisioning. Three provisionings later the
committed ledger still had zero `where` records.

The cause is that the usage spool does not follow `.beads/redirect` the way every other
tracker path does. `br.run_br` records with the `repo_root` it was handed, which for a lane
is the worktree; `tracker_usage.is_enabled` then sees the worktree's own checked-out
`.basicly/ledger/` directory and returns True, so the record is spooled to
`<worktree><redacted:posix-absolute-path>`. The loop deletes the worktree at teardown,
taking the spool with it.

So every engine tracker call made from a worktree is silently discarded. That is not a
uniform sampling loss - it is exactly the traffic the harness generates while doing lane
work, and it makes one surface (`where`) read as never-used when the engine depends on it.

This matters because the ledger is the input to the Phase 6 surface freeze. A false
never-used entry is the worst error that artifact can contain: it would omit a surface the
engine calls on every provisioning.

`br.beads_dir` is the precedent to copy - it follows the redirect file to the base
checkout's `.beads`, whose parent is the base checkout.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Provision a loop worktree, which runs `br where --json` against the worktree path.
2. Run `basicly usage tracker --promote` in the base checkout.
3. Observed: no `where` record, and the report names `where` among the never-used surfaces.
   Expected: `where` recorded as an engine surface.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an engine tracker call made with a linked worktree as its repo root when the record is spooled then it lands in the base checkout's spool so teardown cannot discard it and the surface report counts it

payload.description:
## Context

From the hankweave analysis (`reference-repos/_analysis/hankweave.md`), the only append-only journal
in the reviewed set running in production, measured against its own committed 6,467-event fixture.
Two mechanisms it has and `docs/design/work-tracker.md` does not, plus one measurement that turns a
section 9.5 assertion into evidence.

**1. The denormalized running aggregate.** Every event carries the totals that hold *after* it
(`state.transition.data.resultingState`, `event-schemas.ts:429-434`), so the overwhelmingly common
query - what is the current cost or count - is answered by reading the tail rather than folding the
whole log, while the fold stays available as the checkable authority. Section 4 of our design admits
the cost it does not solve ("a fold is O(events) and a naive reader re-folds per query") and section
10 defers the index by measurement. This is the mechanism that makes deferring the index defensible
rather than a hand-wave, and it costs one field.

**2. Honest truncation.** A large payload is stored truncated with `truncated: true` plus
`originalLength` (`event-schemas.ts:259-268`). Section 9.1 declines lossy compaction on the grounds
that it discards evidence git already packs - which stands - but that leaves growth bounded by
nothing. Truncation with a recorded original length bounds it while *saying* that evidence was
dropped and how much, which is a different and better thing than summarising it away.

**3. Evidence for section 9.5, not a change to it.** Their journal has **no sequence numbers** and
mints ids as `Date.now()` plus `Math.random()` (`utils.ts:26-28`). The analysis measured **44.5% of
events in their production fixture sharing a millisecond**, so total order exists only as an
unrecorded side effect of file append order. Our rule that a timestamp is evidence and nothing
branches on it was asserted; it can now cite a number.

Also record the rejection and why: their sentinels are injected LLM calls with a per-million-token
cost model (`sentinels/sentinel.ts:108`, `:502`), so their monitoring is a paid external API -
inadmissible under `basicly-ctdz`, and `StallWatchdog` already covers the condition that matters.

Net finding worth stating plainly in the design: our unbuilt design is more rigorous than their
shipped one, so this is an absorption of three narrow mechanisms, not a redesign.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the work-tracker design when it is read after this change then the event schema carries a running aggregate with the tail-read query and the fold-as-authority both stated, truncation records originalLength as the growth bound, section 9.5 cites the measured millisecond-collision rate, and the rejected sentinel approach is recorded with its reason
payload.title: Absorb the measured journal mechanisms into the work-tracker design

payload.text: [harness-policy] NARROWED 2026-07-30 on a licence finding (references.md 2.3, basicly-imnu.12). hankweave-runtime is stock Apache-2.0 but its NOTICE.md incorporates Southbridge's Terms of Service, whose key provisions include 'Competition restrictions on using Hanks to build competing products' and 'Managed services restrictions require prior written consent'. basicly is a coding-agent harness and hankweave an agent-orchestration runtime, so the restriction plausibly reaches us, and whether a NOTICE can add terms to Apache-2.0 at all is a legal question we are not qualified to answer. WHAT STAYS IN SCOPE: the measurements, because they are properties of published data rather than derived from code - specifically that 44.5 percent of events in their own committed 6467-event fixture share a millisecond while the journal has no sequence numbers, which turns work-tracker 9.5 from an assertion into evidence, and is the single most valuable thing this bead carries. WHAT IS HELD: adopting the running-aggregate and honest-truncation mechanisms with their source as the reference.
